Creativity Techniques · U6 Creativity and Personal Development

1 · Confidence is practiced

Creative confidence grows from doing creative work — not from waiting to feel gifted.

Gifted, you may feel. Rehearse the method, you must.

(Tao of Creativity)

Image: Van Gogh self-portrait painting.

Vincent van Gogh - Self-Portrait - Google Art Project (454045) · Vincent van Gogh · Public domain · Source

  • Confidence follows action more often than the reverse.
  • U1's teachable creativity claim lands here as habit.
  • Do not confuse performance anxiety with lack of ability.

Source: course wording; Beghetto/Karwowski/Kelley lines still pending page-level citation resolve.

Ask: What did you finish this week that you can point to?

Creativity Techniques · U6 Creativity and Personal Development

2 · Beliefs convert potential

Believing you can and should act creatively turns ability into action under a real brief.

Image: Rembrandt self-portrait etching at a window.

Self-Portrait etching at a window (SM 61530d) · Rembrandt · Public domain · Source

  • Creative confidence and centrality beliefs both matter.
  • Potential without action stays potential.
  • Briefs give a lawful place to act.

Source: course wording.

Ask: Which belief stopped you last month — can, or should?

Creativity Techniques · U6 Creativity and Personal Development

3 · Mastery feeds regulation

Success experiences teach what to repeat, revise, or drop — they train self-regulation.

Image: Vermeer painting of a lady writing at a table.

Johannes Vermeer - A Lady Writing - Google Art Project · Johannes Vermeer · Public domain · Source

  • Mastery here means useful feedback from your own work, not perfection.
  • Regulation is choosing the next move on purpose.
  • Pair with reflection logs, not mood tracking.

Source: course wording.

Ask: What small success will you repeat on purpose next week?

Creativity Techniques · U6 Creativity and Personal Development

4 · Blocks are part of the path

Name blocks; use constraints, peers, and prompts to restart — not shame.

Image: Chardin painting of a boy building a house of cards.

Jean Siméon Chardin, The House of Cards, probably 1737, NGA 97 · Jean-Baptiste-Siméon Chardin · CC0 1.0 · Source

  • Blocks are normal in creative work.
  • Naming beats hiding.
  • Techniques from earlier units are restart tools.

Source: course wording.

Ask: What block name fits your last stall?

Creativity Techniques · U6 Creativity and Personal Development

5 · Sustain beyond the workshop

Personal development means habits under real briefs — not a one-day energy spike.

Image: Vermeer painting of a lady writing a letter with her maid.

Woman writing a letter, with her maid, by Johannes Vermeer · Johannes Vermeer · Public domain · Source

  • Workshop highs fade; portfolios accumulate.
  • Tie practice to course deliverables so it survives the semester.
  • Avoid wellness theatre — stay tied to making and judging.

Source: course wording (C1 adjacency in professor brief).

Ask: Which habit from this course will survive after the exam?

Creativity Techniques · U6 Creativity and Personal Development

6 · Autonomy with accountability

Own your process inside the brief — without romantic isolation.

Image: Friedrich painting of a wanderer above a sea of fog.

Caspar David Friedrich - Wanderer above the sea of fog · Caspar David Friedrich · Public domain · Source

  • Autonomy is self-direction within rules, not ignoring the brief.
  • Accountability includes peers, instructors, and future audiences.
  • Declare AI use and cite influences — same as every unit.

Source: course wording.

Ask: Where do you need a peer voice this week?

Creativity Techniques · U6 Creativity and Personal Development

Recall check

Alone, from memory, 3 minutes. Then compare with a partner.

  1. Does this unit treat confidence as a mood or as practice?
  2. What two beliefs gate creative action?
  3. What should a success experience teach you?
  4. What is the first move when you hit a block?
  5. What outlasts a workshop high?

Course geometric background · threshold · #7a624a21 · Original course SVG

  • Timer: 3 minutes. Students answer alone, from memory; then compare with a partner.
  • Practice only. Nothing is collected or graded.

Answers:

  • 1. Practice — from doing creative work (course wording).
  • 2. Can I do this creatively? Should I act creatively here? (centrality / confidence gates).
  • 3. What to repeat, revise, or drop (regulation).
  • 4. Name the block; use constraints, peers, or prompts to restart.
  • 5. Habits under real briefs / portfolio accumulation.

Ask: Which answer will shape your Lab log today?

Creativity Techniques · U6 Creativity and Personal Development

Exercise 1 · Reflection-in-action log

When something surprises you, stop. Note expectation, event, and the next move — then link the moves after class.

In a good process of design, this conversation with the situation is reflective.

(Schön 1983, 79)

Save at least two surprise stops, the linked end-of-session account, and one line on confidence gained.

Image: 1920 advertisement illustration for modern telephone service.

Modern telephone service for the home. (1920) (14756669655) · Unknown · Public domain · Source

  • Timer: 10 minutes active logging during a shared short making task.
  • Stop when surprised; do not wait until the end to invent a story.
  • After class, link moves into a short account of the conversation with the material.

Source: (Schön 1983, 79); steps are classroom adaptation.

Ask: Which surprise changed your next move?

Creativity Techniques · U6 Creativity and Personal Development

Exercise 2 · Mental locks audit

Recall an idea you dropped early. Name the belief that closed it. Revisit the idea for five minutes with that belief set aside.

Save the dropped idea, the named lock, when the lock helps vs blocks, and what changed in five minutes.

Image: Photograph of a wooden writing desk.

Writing desk · Dvortygirl · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Source

  • Timer: 15 minutes.
  • Private writing is fine; share only what you choose.
  • Do not treat the lock as a character flaw — ask when it helps and when it blocks.

Source: classroom adaptation of Open Mental Locks catalogue records (von Oech held; not in references.yml). Witness urn:in-practice:exercise:0b497d0ff09fe1fe764b1c52.

Ask: Did the reopened idea deserve another session?
